title: Grade 3 Money and Making Change: Rupees, Paise & Shop Bills + Free Quiz
meta_title: Grade 3 Money and Making Change: A Parent Guide
meta_desc: Teach grade 3 money and making change the easy way: convert rupees and paise, add a shop bill, and count up change, with a free 8-question quiz.
excerpt: The kirana shop is the best maths classroom your child already visits. Here is how I teach Grade 3 money and making change, from rupees-and-paise conversion to counting up the change, with a quick quiz to check it stuck.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Grade 3 child a ₹50 note at the stationery shop, let them buy a pencil box for ₹32, and watch what happens when the shopkeeper hands back the change. Most eight-year-olds can tell you 50 minus 32 on paper, but freeze when the coins land in their palm. That gap — between a written sum and real money on a counter — is exactly what grade 3 money and making change is about. It is the year rupees and paise stop being a worksheet exercise and start being something a child can actually do at a shop.

In my experience, the children who get comfortable with money early are not the fastest at arithmetic. They are the ones who have handled real notes and coins, priced a small shopping list, and worked out change by counting up. So most of what follows uses a kirana or stationery shop, because that is where your child already sees rupees change hands.

Rupees and paise: two units, one system

The first thing a Grade 3 child needs solid is the conversion. One rupee is 100 paise. That is the whole rule, and it behaves exactly like rupees and 100 — which is why money is such a natural bridge to place value and, later, decimals.

The confusion is almost always in the writing. ₹5.75 means 5 rupees and 75 paise, not ‘five point seventy-five rupees’ said aloud like a plain number. I get children to read the dot as the word ‘and’: ₹5.75 is ‘five rupees and seventy-five paise’. Once they hear it that way, converting stops being a trick.

AmountIn paiseRead it as
₹1100 paiseone rupee
₹2.50250 paisetwo rupees and fifty paise
₹0.7575 paiseseventy-five paise
₹10.051005 paiseten rupees and five paise

Notice the last row. ₹10.05 trips up nearly every child, because they want to write the 5 paise as ₹10.5. Spend a full session on amounts with a zero in the paise place — ₹20.05, ₹8.09, ₹15.02 — and you will save yourself a term of decimal-point errors later.

Adding up a shopping bill

Once conversion is secure, the next skill is totalling a bill. This is where Grade 3 money gets genuinely useful, because it is a two-step job: add the rupees, add the paise, then carry any hundred of paise into a rupee.

Say a child buys these from the stationery shop:

  • A notebook for ₹24.50
  • A pen for ₹12.75
  • An eraser for ₹5.00

Line them up like ordinary addition, keeping the dots under each other. The paise column is 50 + 75 + 00 = 125 paise, which is 1 rupee and 25 paise — so you write 25 paise and carry 1 rupee. The rupees column is then 24 + 12 + 5 + 1 = 42. The bill is ₹42.25. The habit to drill here is keeping the decimal points in a straight vertical line; a slanted column is where the mistakes hide.

Making change by counting up

Here is the part most worksheets teach badly. To find the change from ₹50 for a ₹42.25 bill, the textbook says ‘subtract’. A real shopkeeper never subtracts. They count up from the price to the amount paid, dropping coins and notes into your hand as they go.

From ₹42.25 to ₹50 looks like this:

StepCount up toCoin or note given
Start at the bill₹42.25—
Fill the paise to a rupee₹4375 paise
Round up to ₹45₹45₹2
Reach the note paid₹50₹5

Add the change given — 75 paise + ₹2 + ₹5 = ₹7.75. Check it against the subtraction, 50 − 42.25 = 7.75, and they match. Counting up feels slower to write out, but it is how change actually works, and children make far fewer errors this way because each step is a small, friendly jump rather than one scary borrow across a decimal point.

Why counting up beats borrowing

Subtracting ₹42.25 from ₹50 on paper means borrowing across the decimal — a genuinely hard move for an eight-year-old. Counting up sidesteps the borrowing entirely. It also builds a mental picture of the number line that pays off in Grade 4 and 5. If your child can only do one method well, make it this one.

A weekly routine that actually works

Ten minutes of real money beats an hour of worksheets. A rhythm I have seen work: keep a small tin of coins and a few play notes at home. Two days a week, set up a pretend shop — price three items, let the child total the bill and make change. One day, practise pure rupee-paise conversion. One day, written questions on paper so they learn to lay out the decimal points neatly. The weekend is for a real trip: hand them the money at the shop and let them check the change themselves.

One honest caveat: do not rush to decimals-as-abstract-numbers. A child who can make change with real coins understands ₹7.75 far better than one who has only ever seen it written. The concrete comes first; the abstract follows on its own.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

Below is a free 8-question quiz on exactly these skills — converting rupees and paise, totalling a shop bill, and making change by counting up. Let your child try it and read the explanations together for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end has graded money questions with a full answer key you can print as often as you like.

quiz.title: Grade 3 Money & Making Change Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on rupees and paise, adding a shop bill, and making change. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 3 money, rupee-paise conversion and change

questions.q: How many paise are there in 1 rupee?
questions.explanation: One rupee is always 100 paise, just like one hundred is 100 ones.
₹2 is 200 paise, plus 50 paise more, which makes 250 paise.

questions.q: How do you write ‘ten rupees and five paise’ with a rupee symbol?
questions.explanation: Five paise fills only the last place, so it is written ₹10.05. Writing ₹10.5 would mean fifty paise.

questions.q: A notebook costs ₹24.50 and a pen costs ₹12.75. What is the total bill?
questions.explanation: The paise are 50 + 75 = 125 paise = 1 rupee 25 paise. So 24 + 12 + 1 = 37 rupees and 25 paise, or ₹37.25.

questions.q: You pay ₹50 for a bill of ₹42. How much change should you get?
questions.explanation: Count up from 42 to 50: that is 8 rupees. So the change is ₹8.

questions.q: Counting up to make change from ₹20 for a ₹15.50 bill, what do you add first to reach a whole rupee?
questions.explanation: First fill the paise: from ₹15.50 add 50 paise to reach ₹16, then carry on up to ₹20.

questions.q: What is the change from ₹100 for a bill of ₹73?
Which coins and notes make exactly ₹7.75 in change?

faq.q: What money skills should a Grade 3 child know?
faq.a: By the end of Grade 3 a child should convert between rupees and paise (₹1 = 100 paise), read amounts like ₹5.75 correctly, add up a small shop bill with rupees and paise, and make change from a round amount. Handling real coins matters as much as the written sums.

faq.q: How do I explain rupees and paise to my child?
faq.a: Keep it to one rule: one rupee is 100 paise. Read the dot in ₹5.75 as the word ‘and’ — ‘five rupees and seventy-five paise’. Practise amounts with a zero in the paise place, like ₹10.05, because those are the ones children get wrong most.

faq.q: What is the easiest way to make change?
faq.a: Count up from the price to the amount paid, the way a shopkeeper does, instead of subtracting. For a ₹42 bill paid with ₹50, count 42 up to 50, which is ₹8. It avoids borrowing across the decimal point and children make far fewer mistakes.

faq.q: Why does my child struggle with amounts like ₹10.05?
faq.a: They read the 5 as fifty paise and want to write ₹10.5. The paise part always needs two places, so five paise is written 05. Spend a session only on amounts with a zero in the tens-of-paise place and it clicks quickly.
